title: Catholic: the saints
hook: Catholics speak of the communion of saints, friends in heaven who pray with the living (Hebrews 12:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rosary, prayers counted in decades. Your line was one bead at a time.

The last mile of a marathon. Your legs are gone. You're sure you can't finish. Then you hear it: the crowd along the barriers, thousands of strangers shouting your name off the bib on your chest. Somehow you keep going. Now imagine that crowd isn't strangers. It's everyone who ran this course before you, who hit the same wall and got through, still watching, still cheering. That's close to how Catholics picture the saints. Today: the communion of saints.
screen: `THE LAST MILE OF A MARATHON.` → `A CROWD SHOUTING YOUR NAME.` → `EVERYONE WHO RAN IT BEFORE.`

segments.voice: The picture comes from the letter to the Hebrews. After a long list of faithful people from the Hebrew Bible, Abraham, Sarah, Moses and more, the writer says, in the King James Version: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight." And run the race. A cloud, meaning a great crowd; witnesses, people who've seen it through. Saint comes from the Latin sanctus, holy. In the New Testament, Paul calls all believers saints. Over time the Church also began to honor particular people, first the martyrs, then others, whose lives showed holiness clearly, and today Catholics recognize some of them formally through a long process called canonization. The Apostles' Creed, said by many Christians, includes the line I believe in the communion of saints. For Catholics that means the Church isn't only the people in the pews: it includes those who have died in Christ, and the bond isn't broken by death. So Catholics ask the saints to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend. They're careful to say they honor saints and ask for their prayers; worship belongs to God alone. There are patron saints for almost everything: Francis for animals, Anthony for lost things, Joseph for workers and fathers. Christians differ here. Orthodox Christians also honor the saints and ask their prayers, often through icons. Many Protestants honor faithful people of the past as examples, but don't ask them to pray, preferring to pray to God directly. Either way, the old letter's picture holds: you are not the first to run this.
screen: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.` · `SANCTUS — HOLY.` · `DEATH DOESN'T BREAK THE BOND.` · `HONORED, ASKED TO PRAY, NOT WORSHIPED.` · then, large: `A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Let your own cloud of witnesses gather: a grandparent, a teacher, someone from history, a saint if you have one, people who ran their race with courage or kindness. Choose one, and picture their face, or what you know of it. What would they say to you, in your last hard mile?
Catholic, through the saints: the communion of saints, a great cloud of witnesses who, Catholics believe, still pray with the living. Today's word.
Your line: a cloud of witnesses. The crowd at the barriers is bigger than it looks. That's day two hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate saints' feast days through the year and All Saints' Day on November 1, take a saint's name at confirmation, and ask saints to pray for them, often through a patron saint.
